question: What is minidis, and what does it mean that it is "wire compatible" with Redis?
answer_hinglish:
minidis ek in-memory key-value database hai jo maine Python asyncio mein scratch se likha, aur yeh wahi protocol bolta hai jo real Redis bolta hai -- RESP (REdis Serialization Protocol). "Wire compatible" ka matlab hai ki TCP pe jo bytes jaate aur aate hain, woh Redis jaise hi hain. Isliye official `redis-py` client, `redis-cli` aur `redis-benchmark` bina ek line change kiye minidis se baat kar lete hain.

Yeh claim main hawa mein nahi karta: poora test suite (52 tests) official redis-py client se real server pe chalta hai -- har test `port=0` pe ek naya server start karta hai aur `redis.asyncio.Redis` se commands bhejta hai. Matlab har passing test protocol compatibility ka proof bhi hai. Benchmarks bhi real `redis-benchmark` (C binary) se liye, jo protocol mein zara bhi galti ho toh turant toot jaata.

Scope honest rakhna zaroori hai: strings, keys/TTL, lists, sets, hashes, persistence (snapshot + AOF), replication aur INFO hai. MULTI/EXEC, Pub/Sub, Lua, sorted sets, streams, cluster -- yeh nahi hain. Goal Redis ki performance match karna nahi tha, balki Redis ke andar ke mechanisms (atomicity, expiry, eviction, durability, replication) ko khud implement karke samajhna tha.
why_needed: Wire compatibility ka fayda yeh hai ki khud ka client likhne ki zaroorat nahi, aur battle-tested clients se testing hoti hai jo protocol bugs turant pakad lete hain.
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek naya ATM jo kisi bhi bank ka card accept karta hai kyunki woh same card protocol follow karta hai -- andar ki machine alag hai, lekin interface standard.
how_it_works:
Client TCP connection kholta hai, RESP arrays bhejta hai (`*2
$3
GET
$1
k
`), server parse karke command chalata hai aur RESP reply (`$1
v
`) bhejta hai. Jab tak bytes ka format same hai, client ko pata hi nahi chalta ki peeche C wala Redis hai ya Python wala minidis.
in_this_project: `minidis/protocol.py` mein `Parser` aur `encode()` hain; `tests/conftest.py` ka `running()` context manager real `Server` start karta hai aur `client_for()` redis-py client deta hai. `bench/compare.sh` same Docker network mein real Redis 7 aur minidis dono pe `redis-benchmark` chalata hai.
advantages: Tests automatically protocol compatibility prove karte hain
Real tools (redis-cli, redis-benchmark) se debugging aur benchmarking
disadvantages: Protocol ki saari quirks follow karni padti hain (jaise BGSAVE SCHEDULE, HELLO 3)
Clients jo commands assume karte hain (COMMAND DOCS) unka stub dena padta hai
common_mistakes: Yeh claim karna ki minidis poora Redis hai -- sirf ek subset hai
Sirf apne likhe client se test karna, jo same galti dono taraf chhupa deta hai
follow_up_questions: Kaunse commands implement nahi kiye aur kyun?
redis-py 8 se connect karte waqt kya problem aayi thi?
Wire compatibility test kaise karte ho?

question: TCP is a byte stream. What does that mean for a server that reads commands from clients?
answer_hinglish:
TCP reliable aur ordered bytes deta hai, lekin message boundaries nahi deta. Client ne do `send()` kiye toh server ko ek `read()` mein dono mil sakte hain; client ne ek bada command bheja toh woh teen `read()` mein toot ke aa sakta hai. TCP ke liye sab ek lambi byte ki nadi hai -- "yahan ek command khatam hua" yeh batana application protocol ka kaam hai. Isko framing kehte hain.

Iska seedha consequence: server yeh assume nahi kar sakta ki `reader.read(65536)` ne exactly ek command diya. Agar naive code har read ko ek command maan le, toh pipelining pe sirf pehla command chalega, aur bade values pe aadha command parse hoke garbage banega.

minidis mein `_handle_client` jo bhi bytes aaye unhe `parser.feed(data)` se buffer mein daalta hai, phir loop mein `parser.get_command()` call karta hai jab tak woh `None` na de. `None` ka matlab "abhi poora command nahi aaya, aur bytes ka wait karo". Ek read mein 16 commands aaye toh loop 16 baar chalega; aadha command aaya toh zero baar, aur bacha hua hissa buffer mein agle read ka wait karega. `test_partial_frames_are_buffered_until_complete` command ko ek-ek byte karke feed karta hai aur aakhri byte tak `None` hi milta hai.
why_needed: Bina framing ke koi bhi TCP server pipelining aur bade payloads pe randomly fail karega -- aur yeh bug sirf load ya slow network pe dikhta hai, local testing mein nahi.
real_world_analogy: Jaise courier se kitaab ke pages alag-alag packets mein aa rahe hain; jab tak last page na aaye, chapter padhna shuru nahi kar sakte. Aur kabhi ek packet mein do chapters ke pages ek saath aa jaate hain.
how_it_works: Framing do tarah se hoti hai: delimiter (jaise newline) ya length prefix. RESP dono use karta hai: header lines `\r\n` pe khatam hoti hain, aur bulk strings ke pehle `$<len>` aata hai, toh exactly utne bytes padhne hain.
in_this_project: `Server._handle_client` mein `data = await reader.read(65536)`, phir `parser.feed(data)` aur `while (args := parser.get_command()) is not None:` loop. `Parser.pending` batata hai kitne bytes buffer mein bache hain -- replica side pe isi se replication offset count hota hai.
code_example:
# real, trimmed: minidis/server.py::_handle_client
data = await reader.read(65536)
if not data:
    break
parser.feed(data)
while (args := parser.get_command()) is not None:
    ...
    replies.append(encode(self.execute(args, client), client.proto))
advantages: Pipelining aur partial reads dono naturally handle hote hain
Ek read mein jitne commands aaye sab ek batch mein process
disadvantages: Buffer memory leta hai; bina limits ke malicious client bada buffer bana sakta hai
common_mistakes: Ek read() = ek message maan lena
UDP aur TCP ki semantics confuse karna
Local testing pe pass hone ko proof maan lena
follow_up_questions: Length-prefix vs delimiter framing ke kya trade-offs hain?
Buffer unbounded grow kare toh kya karoge?
Nagle's algorithm ka is pe kya asar hai?

question: Explain the RESP format. How is a command like GET k encoded on the wire, and what reply types exist?
answer_hinglish:
RESP ek simple text-ish protocol hai jisme har value ka pehla byte uska type batata hai. RESP2 mein paanch types hain: `+` simple string (`+OK
`), `-` error (`-ERR message
`), `:` integer (`:42
`), `$` bulk string (`$5
hello
`, aur `$-1
` null), aur `*` array (`*2
...`).

Clients commands hamesha array of bulk strings ki tarah bhejte hain. `GET k` wire pe aisa dikhta hai: `*2
$3
GET
$1
k
` -- "2 elements ka array, pehla 3 bytes ka GET, doosra 1 byte ka k". Reply agar value `v` hai toh `$1
v
`, key nahi hai toh `$-1
` (RESP2 null) ya RESP3 mein `_
`.

Design ki khoobi: length pehle aati hai, isliye parser ko value ke andar delimiter dhoondhna nahi padta -- value mein `
` ya null byte ho tab bhi chalega. Aur format itna simple hai ki telnet se bhi debug kar sakte ho.

minidis mein `protocol.py` ke top docstring mein yahi recap hai. `encode_command(args)` kisi bhi command ko array-of-bulk-strings mein badalta hai -- isi function se AOF file aur replication stream bhi likhe jaate hain, matlab teeno jagah (client wire, disk, replica) same format hai.
why_needed: Protocol samjhe bina na parser likh sakte ho, na Wireshark/tcpdump se production issue debug kar sakte ho.
real_world_analogy: Jaise courier box pe pehle label: "andar 3 items hain, pehla 5 kg ka" -- kholne wala bina andar jhaanke jaanta hai kab ruk na hai.
how_it_works: Har line `\r\n` pe khatam. Bulk string: `$` + length + CRLF + exactly length bytes + CRLF. Array: `*` + count + CRLF + count elements (jo khud bhi koi bhi type ho sakte hain -- nested).
in_this_project: `protocol.py::encode` Python types se mapping karta hai: `SimpleString` -> `+`, `RespError` -> `-`, `int` -> `:`, `bytes` -> `$`, `list` -> `*`, `None` -> `$-1` ya `_`. `encode_command` AOF (`aof.py`) aur `_propagate` mein use hota hai. `DATABASE_DESIGN.md` mein AOF ka example literally RESP bytes hai.
code_example:
# real: minidis/protocol.py
def encode_command(args):
    out = [b"*", str(len(args)).encode(), b"
"]
    for a in args:
        out += [b"$", str(len(a)).encode(), b"
", a, b"
"]
    return b"".join(out)
# encode_command([b"GET", b"k"]) == b"*2
$3
GET
$1
k
"
advantages: Human readable aur parse karna aasaan
Ek hi format client, AOF aur replication mein
disadvantages: Text integers parse karne padte hain (binary protocols se thoda slow)
RESP2 mein types kam hain, map/set ka fark client ko khud samajhna padta hai
common_mistakes: Null bulk ($-1) aur empty string ($0) ko same samajhna
Simple string mein binary data bhejna -- woh binary safe nahi hai
follow_up_questions: RESP3 mein kya naye types aaye?
Inline commands kya hote hain?
Error prefix (WRONGTYPE, READONLY) ka kya role hai?

question: What is an in-memory database, and how does minidis still provide durability?
answer_hinglish:
In-memory database ka matlab hai ki poora dataset RAM mein rehta hai aur har read/write RAM pe hota hai -- disk pe nahi. Isliye latency microseconds mein hoti hai, disk seek ka koi chakkar nahi. Lekin RAM volatile hai: process crash ya machine restart hua toh sab gaya. Isliye "in-memory" aur "durable" alag dimensions hain, aur durability ek dial hai jo operator set karta hai.

minidis mein yeh dial `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` ki table mein hai: koi persistence nahi (sab lose), sirf snapshots (last snapshot ke baad ka sab lose), AOF `no` (jo OS ne flush nahi kiya -- Linux pe typically ~30s tak), AOF `everysec` (~1s), aur AOF `always` (koi bhi acknowledged write lose nahi). Disk sirf persistence ke liye hai; reads kabhi disk se nahi hote.

Cache aur database mein fark bhi yahi se aata hai. Cache use-case mein data kahin aur se rebuild ho sakta hai, toh `allkeys-lru` eviction aur weak durability chalega. Primary store ke liye `noeviction` aur AOF `everysec`/`always` chahiye. `DEPLOYMENT.md` yahi recommend karta hai.

Interview mein main yeh bolta hoon: RAM speed deti hai, persistence correctness ka level, aur dono ke beech trade-off explicitly choose karna padta hai -- default kuch bhi "free" nahi hai.
why_needed: Har architecture discussion mein poocha jaata hai ki Redis pe data rakhna safe hai ya nahi; iska jawab persistence mode pe depend karta hai, "haan/nahi" nahi.
real_world_analogy: Jaise whiteboard pe kaam karna (fast) aur har ghante phone se photo lena (snapshot) ya har line ek notebook mein bhi likhna (AOF) -- kitni baar likhte ho, utna kam khona padega.
how_it_works: Writes RAM mein data structures update karte hain; saath mein AOF buffer mein command append hota hai aur policy ke hisaab se fsync hota hai. Snapshots periodically poore dataset ko file mein serialize karte hain. Restart pe AOF replay ya snapshot load se RAM wapas bharta hai.
in_this_project: `config.py::ServerConfig` mein `appendonly=False` aur `save_rules=[(3600,1),(300,100),(60,10000)]` defaults hain. Dockerfile ka CMD `--appendonly yes` deta hai. `server.py::_load_from_disk` restart pe data wapas laata hai.
disadvantages: Dataset RAM size se bada nahi ho sakta
Strong durability (always) throughput kam karta hai
Restart pe load time dataset size ke saath badhta hai
common_mistakes: Yeh maan lena ki in-memory DB matlab data hamesha lose hoga
Yeh maan lena ki AOF on hai toh zero loss -- fsync policy dekhni padti hai
follow_up_questions: everysec mein exactly kitna data lose ho sakta hai?
Snapshot aur AOF dono on hon toh restart pe kya load hota hai?
Dataset RAM se bada ho jaye toh?

question: How do TTL and key expiration work from a user's point of view? What do TTL and PTTL return?
answer_hinglish:
TTL (time to live) se key ko ek expiry deadline milti hai; deadline ke baad key logically exist nahi karti. Commands: `EXPIRE k 60` (seconds), `PEXPIRE` (ms), `EXPIREAT`/`PEXPIREAT` (absolute unix time), `SET k v EX 60`, aur `PERSIST k` jo TTL hata deta hai.

`TTL` aur `PTTL` ke return values yaad rakhne layak hain: `-2` matlab key exist hi nahi karti, `-1` matlab key hai lekin uski koi expiry nahi, warna bacha hua time. minidis mein `TTL` nearest second pe round karta hai: `(p + 500) // 1000`, jaise Redis.

Kuch semantics jo log galat samajhte hain, aur code mein follow kiye gaye hain: plain `SET` purana TTL hata deta hai (`store(..., keep_ttl=False)` andar `persist` call karta hai) jab tak `KEEPTTL` na diya ho; `INCR` aur `APPEND` TTL rakhte hain (`keep_ttl=True`); past time ka `EXPIRE` key turant delete karta hai aur `DEL` propagate karta hai, past `PEXPIREAT` nahi.

Andar se har expiry absolute unix milliseconds mein `Keyspace.expires` dict mein store hoti hai. Relative TTL sirf input format hai -- storage aur AOF dono mein absolute time jaata hai, jisse replay deterministic rehta hai.
why_needed: Sessions, OTPs, rate limit windows, cache entries -- sab TTL pe depend karte hain; galat semantics (jaise SET se TTL hatna) production bugs banate hain.
real_world_analogy: Jaise dukaan ka coupon jispe expiry date likhi hai -- date nikal gayi toh coupon bekaar, chahe drawer mein pada ho.
how_it_works: Expiry absolute ms timestamp hai. Har access pe check (lazy) aur background sampling (active) se expired keys hat ti hain. TTL query current time se difference nikalti hai.
in_this_project: `commands/keys.py::ttl` rounding karta hai, `Keyspace.pttl` -2/-1 logic. `_expire_generic` past deadline pe `ctx.ks.delete(key)` aur `ctx.rewrite([b"DEL", key])`. `test_ttl_semantics` aur `test_set_options` yeh behaviour verify karte hain.
advantages: Automatic cleanup bina application code ke
disadvantages: Expiry exactly deadline pe memory free nahi karti (lazy + sampled)
Clock jump (NTP) absolute deadlines ko affect karta hai
common_mistakes: SET se TTL reset hona bhool jana
TTL -1 aur -2 mein confuse hona
Expired key ko turant memory se gaya maan lena

Replica pe TTL kaise kaam karta hai?

question: What is pipelining, and why does it increase throughput so much?
answer_hinglish:
Pipelining ka matlab hai client bina reply ka wait kiye kai commands ek saath bhej deta hai, aur baad mein saare replies padhta hai. Bina pipelining ke har command ek full network round-trip (RTT) leta hai: send, wait, receive. Agar RTT 0.5ms hai toh ek connection pe maximum ~2000 commands/second, chahe server kitna bhi fast ho. Pipelining mein N commands ek RTT mein chale jaate hain, aur server side pe bhi per-command overhead (syscalls, wakeups) amortize hota hai.

minidis ka benchmark yeh clearly dikhata hai (TESTING.md, redis-benchmark, -n 50000 -c 50, shared Docker Desktop machine): replication fix ke baad SET P=1 pe 8,169 req/s tha aur P=16 pe 34,698 req/s; GET 13,277 se 53,135. Real Redis ke liye bhi SET 30,102 se 207,469 gaya.

Server side pe minidis pipelining ka poora fayda uthata hai: ek `read()` mein jitne commands aaye sab parse aur execute hote hain, replies ek list mein jama hote hain, aur end mein `writer.write(b"".join(replies))` -- ek hi write. AOF `always` mode mein bhi poore batch ke liye ek fsync hota hai (group commit). `test_pipelining` 1000 SET ek pipeline mein bhejta hai.

Important nuance: pipelining transaction nahi hai. Beech mein doosre clients ke commands interleave ho sakte hain; atomicity sirf individual command level pe hai.
why_needed: High throughput systems (bulk loads, counters) mein RTT hi bottleneck hota hai; pipelining sabse sasta 5-10x jeet hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise dukaan pe ek ek item mangwa ke har baar counter pe wapas aana vs poori list ek baar de dena.
how_it_works: Client socket pe N commands likhta hai; server ka parser buffer se ek ek nikalta hai, execute karta hai, replies batch karke ek write mein bhejta hai. Client replies ko order mein match karta hai (RESP ordered hai).
in_this_project: `_handle_client` mein `replies: list[bytes]` aur end mein ek `writer.write` + `await writer.drain()`. `tests/test_concurrency.py::test_pipelining` redis-py `pipeline(transaction=False)` use karta hai. `bench/compare.sh` P=1 aur P=16 dono chalata hai.
code_example:
# real: tests/test_concurrency.py
async with c.pipeline(transaction=False) as p:
    for i in range(1000):
        p.set(f"k{i}", i)
    res = await p.execute()
advantages: Server pe ek write/fsync per batch
disadvantages: Atomic nahi -- doosre clients interleave kar sakte hain
Bahut bade pipelines server/client buffers badhate hain
Ek command fail hone se baaki rukte nahi
common_mistakes: Pipelining ko MULTI/EXEC transaction samajhna
Unbounded pipeline bana ke memory blow karna
follow_up_questions: Pipelining aur MULTI/EXEC mein kya fark hai?
Server side pe ek batch ke replies ek write mein kyun bhejte ho?

question: What is the asyncio event loop, and how does minidis use it to serve many clients?
answer_hinglish:
asyncio Python ka single-threaded concurrency model hai. Ek event loop hota hai jo bahut saare tasks (coroutines) ko chalata hai; jab koi task I/O ka wait karta hai (`await reader.read()`), loop doosre ready task ko chala deta hai. OS ke `select/epoll/IOCP` se loop jaanta hai kaunsa socket ready hai. Isse ek hi thread hazaron idle connections handle kar leta hai, kyunki waiting mein CPU nahi lagta.

minidis mein `Server.start()` `asyncio.start_server(self._handle_client, host, port)` call karta hai. Har naye TCP connection ke liye asyncio `_handle_client` ka ek naya task banata hai -- "one task per connection". Woh task `read`, parse, execute, `write`, `drain` loop karta hai. Saath mein ek `_cron` task chalta hai (10Hz housekeeping), aur replica mode mein `ReplicaLink._run` task.

Key point: tasks parallel nahi chalte, interleave hote hain -- aur sirf `await` points pe switch hota hai. Yahi minidis ki atomicity ka base hai: command handlers sync functions hain, unke andar koi `await` nahi, toh ek command ke beech mein doosra client nahi aa sakta. `test_many_concurrent_clients` 200 concurrent connections se SET karta hai aur sab sahi aata hai.

Downside: CPU-heavy kaam (bada KEYS, snapshot serialization) loop ko block karta hai aur sab clients rukte hain.
why_needed: Redis bhi single-threaded event loop (ae.c) pe hai; isko samjhe bina Redis ki performance aur atomicity guarantees samajh nahi aati.
real_world_analogy: Ek waiter jo bahut tables sambhalta hai: jab tak ek table menu padh rahi hai, woh doosri table ka order le leta hai. Lekin agar woh ek table pe 10 minute baat karne lage, sab tables wait karengi.
how_it_works: Loop: ready callbacks chalao -> I/O poll karo -> jinke sockets ready hain unke futures resolve karo -> unke tasks resume. Koi task sirf `await` pe control wapas deta hai (cooperative multitasking).
in_this_project: `Server.start` mein `asyncio.start_server` aur `asyncio.create_task(self._cron(), name="cron")`. `ClientState` har connection ka state (id, proto, commands count) rakhta hai, `self.clients` dict mein. `__main__.py` `asyncio.run(main())` se sab start karta hai.
code_example:
# real, trimmed: minidis/server.py
self._server = await asyncio.start_server(self._handle_client, self.config.host, self.config.port)
self._tasks.append(asyncio.create_task(self._cron(), name="cron"))
disadvantages: Sirf ek CPU core use hota hai
Koi bhi blocking call sab ko rokti hai
CPU-bound kaam ke liye unsuitable
common_mistakes: Async ko parallel samajhna
Handler mein time.sleep ya heavy CPU kaam daal dena
Har connection ke liye thread banana jab asyncio kaafi hai

question: How does the minidis RESP parser handle partial frames? Walk through what happens when half a command arrives.
answer_hinglish:
Parser ka rule simple hai: bytes buffer mein jodte jao, aur buffer se kuch bhi tab tak consume mat karo jab tak poora command available na ho. Agar beech mein kahin bhi data kam pada, `None` return karo aur buffer waise ka waisa chhod do.

`_parse_multibulk` step by step: pehle `*<count>\r\n` header ka `\r\n` dhoondhta hai -- nahi mila toh `None`. Phir har argument ke liye: position pe `$` hona chahiye (nahi toh `ProtocolError`), length line ka `\r\n` dhoondho (nahi mila toh `None`), length parse karo, aur check karo ki `start + length + 2` bytes buffer mein hain ya nahi -- nahi hain toh `None` with comment "payload not fully arrived yet". Sirf jab saare arguments mil gaye, tab `del buf[:pos]` se ek saath consume.

Iska fayda: parser ko koi intermediate state (jaise "main teesre argument pe tha") yaad nahi rakhni padti; har call start se dobara parse karta hai. Trade-off: ek bahut bada command jo dheere-dheere aa raha hai, uska header baar baar parse hota hai -- O(n) per read. Redis andar `bulklen`/`multibulklen` jaisa state rakh ke yeh rescan bachata hai.

Proof: `test_partial_frames_are_buffered_until_complete` `SET key "hello world"` ko ek-ek byte feed karta hai; aakhri byte se pehle har baar `None`, aakhri byte pe poora command, aur `pending == 0`.
why_needed: Real network pe bade values aur slow clients ke saath partial reads normal hain; parser inko handle na kare toh random corruption hota hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise jigsaw puzzle ka dabba: jab tak saare pieces nahi aaye, tasveer frame mein nahi lagate -- aur pieces ko table se uthate bhi nahi.
how_it_works: Stateless re-parse: har `get_command()` buffer ke start se parse karta hai, positions local variable `pos` mein, aur success pe hi buffer trim. Pipelined data mein loop dobara `get_command()` call karta hai agle command ke liye.
in_this_project: `protocol.py::Parser._parse_multibulk`, `Parser.feed`, `Parser.pending`. Buffer `bytearray` hai taaki `+=` aur `del buf[:pos]` in-place ho. Replica side `replication.py` mein `before - parser.pending` se consumed bytes gin ke offset badhata hai.
code_example:
# real, trimmed: minidis/protocol.py
start = line_end + 2
if len(buf) < start + length + 2:
    return None  # payload not fully arrived yet
args.append(bytes(buf[start:start + length]))
pos = start + length + 2
...
del buf[:pos]  # consume only now that the whole command is present
return args
advantages: Simple aur bug-free: koi partial state nahi
disadvantages: Bade slow-arriving commands pe header rescan (quadratic-ish worst case)
`del buf[:pos]` bytearray ke front se delete karta hai, jo baaki bytes shift karta hai
common_mistakes: Length check mein trailing `\r\n` ke 2 bytes bhool jana
Partial parse pe buffer ka hissa consume kar dena
Ek read = ek command maan lena
follow_up_questions: Redis ka parser stateful kyun hai?
Malformed input pe kya hota hai?
512MB bulk string aaye toh memory pe kya asar?

question: Why is RESP binary safe, and how do you prove minidis handles binary values correctly?
answer_hinglish:
Binary safe ka matlab hai value mein koi bhi byte ho sakti hai -- `\r\n`, null byte `\x00`, invalid UTF-8 -- aur woh bina corrupt hue store aur wapas mil jaye. RESP bulk strings length-prefixed hain: `$7\r\n` bolta hai "agle exactly 7 bytes value hain". Parser value ke andar delimiter dhoondhta hi nahi, sirf length jitne bytes slice karta hai. Isliye value mein `\r\n` aaye toh bhi koi confusion nahi.

Contrast: inline commands aur simple strings (`+OK`) binary safe nahi hain, kyunki woh newline/space pe split hote hain. Isliye minidis `SimpleString` sirf fixed words (OK, PONG, type names) ke liye use karta hai, user data hamesha bulk string (`bytes`) ki tarah jaata hai.

Code level pe minidis puri tarah bytes mein kaam karta hai: keys aur values Python `bytes` hain, decode kahin nahi hota (sirf command name ko upper karke registry lookup ke liye, aur KEYS/SCAN pattern matching ke liye `decode("utf-8", "replace")`). Snapshot format bhi length-prefixed blobs (`_blob`: u32 length + bytes) use karta hai, toh disk pe bhi binary safety bani rehti hai.

Proof: `test_binary_safe_values` value `b"a\r\nb\x00c"` ke saath SET encode karta hai aur parse ke baad exactly wahi bytes milte hain.
why_needed: Users images, protobufs, compressed blobs, ya serialized objects store karte hain; ek bhi byte bigdi toh data corrupt.
real_world_analogy: Jaise envelope pe likha ho "andar 7 pages hain" -- andar ke pages pe kuch bhi likha ho, ginti se pata hai kahan khatam.
how_it_works: Length prefix + raw bytes + CRLF terminator (jo sirf sanity ke liye hai, value ka hissa nahi). Encoder `len(value)` bytes mein ginta hai, characters mein nahi.
in_this_project: `protocol.py::encode` mein `bytes` branch `$` + `len(value)` likhti hai; `_parse_multibulk` `buf[start:start + length]` slice karta hai. `snapshot.py::_blob` disk pe same idea. Test: `tests/test_protocol.py::test_binary_safe_values`.
code_example:
# real: tests/test_protocol.py
def test_binary_safe_values():
    p = Parser()
    value = b"a\r\nb\x00c"
    p.feed(encode_command([b"SET", b"k", value]))
    assert p.get_command()[2] == value
advantages: Koi bhi data store ho sakta hai
disadvantages: Length text mein hai, toh parse karna padta hai
Inline/simple string paths binary safe nahi
common_mistakes: Length ko characters mein ginna (UTF-8 multibyte pe galat)
Keys ko str mein decode karke store karna
Simple string mein user data bhejna

KEYS pattern matching mein decode kyun kiya?
Snapshot format binary safety kaise maintain karta hai?

question: What are inline commands, and why does minidis support them?
answer_hinglish:
Inline command woh hai jo RESP array ke bajaye ek plain text line ki tarah aata hai: `PING\r\n` ya `SET a 1\r\n`. Yeh mainly humans ke liye hai -- telnet ya `nc` se server se baat karte waqt array format haath se likhna mushkil hai. Real Redis bhi inline commands support karta hai, aur production debugging mein "telnet se PING karke dekho" kaafi common hai.

minidis mein `get_command()` pehla byte dekhta hai: `*` hai toh `_parse_multibulk`, warna `_parse_inline`. Inline parser `\n` dhoondhta hai; nahi mila toh `None` (abhi line poori nahi) -- lekin agar buffer `MAX_INLINE_LEN` (64KB) se bada ho gaya bina newline ke, toh `ProtocolError("too big inline request")`. Yeh important hai, warna koi client bina newline ke bytes bhejta rahe aur buffer infinite grow kare. Line mili toh trailing `\r` strip, whitespace pe split. Khali line (sirf Enter) aaye toh recursively agla command try karta hai.

Limitation: inline split whitespace pe hota hai, toh value mein space ya binary data nahi bhej sakte -- yeh binary safe nahi hai. Real clients (redis-py, redis-cli) hamesha RESP arrays bhejte hain, toh yeh sirf debugging convenience hai.

Test: `test_inline_command` `PING\r\nSET a  1\r\n` feed karta hai (double space bhi) aur `[b"PING"]`, `[b"SET", b"a", b"1"]` milta hai.
why_needed: Ops engineers ke liye telnet se health check karna bina client install kiye -- aur hidden DoS vector (newline-less flood) ko limit karna.
real_world_analogy: Jaise bank mein form bharna (RESP) vs counter pe seedha bol dena (inline) -- chhote kaam ke liye bolna kaafi, lekin complex cheez form se hi.
how_it_works: First byte se dispatch; inline mode mein newline-delimited line, `split()` se args. Size limit sirf tab check hota hai jab newline nahi mila.
in_this_project: `protocol.py::_parse_inline` aur `MAX_INLINE_LEN = 64 * 1024`. `SECURITY.md` is limit ko memory exhaustion mitigation ki list mein rakhta hai.
disadvantages: Binary safe nahi
Quoting support nahi (Redis inline mein quotes handle karta hai)
common_mistakes: Inline parser pe size limit lagana bhool jana
Inline ko production clients ke liye use karna
follow_up_questions: Inline parser mein 64KB limit kyun?
Khali line pe recursion ka kya risk hai?
Redis inline quoting kaise handle karta hai?

question: What is the difference between RESP2 and RESP3, and how does HELLO negotiation work in minidis?
answer_hinglish:
RESP2 mein sirf paanch types hain, isliye bahut si cheezein ambiguous hain: `HGETALL` ek flat array `[f1, v1, f2, v2]` deta hai aur client ko pata hona chahiye ki pairs banane hain; `SMEMBERS` ek array deta hai, set nahi; null ke do forms hain (`$-1` aur `*-1`). RESP3 typed replies laata hai: map `%`, set `~`, null `_`, boolean `#`, double `,` -- client generic tarike se sahi Python type bana sakta hai.

Negotiation per connection hota hai. Client `HELLO 3` bhejta hai; server agar support karta hai toh us connection ka protocol 3 ho jaata hai aur server info map return hota hai. `HELLO 4` jaisa unsupported version aaye toh `NOPROTO` error.

minidis ka design: commands protocol ke baare mein kuch nahi jaante. Woh Python types return karte hain -- `dict` (hash), `RespSet` (set), `None`, `bool`, `float` -- aur `encode(value, proto)` client ke `ClientState.proto` ke hisaab se wire form chunta hai. Ek subtle detail: `_handle_client` mein `encode(self.execute(args, client), client.proto)` likha hai; Python mein arguments left-to-right evaluate hote hain, toh `execute` (jo HELLO handler mein proto set karta hai) pehle chalta hai aur HELLO 3 ka reply khud RESP3 map mein jaata hai -- jo client expect karta hai.

Yeh feature ek real bug se aaya: redis-py 8 by default `HELLO 3` bhejta hai, aur minidis pehle sirf RESP2 bolta tha, toh har connection fail ho raha tha.
why_needed: Modern clients RESP3 by default use karte hain; support na ho toh server unusable hai. Aur typed replies se client code simple hota hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise do log pehle decide karte hain "Hindi mein baat karein ya English mein" -- ek baar tay hua toh poori baatcheet usi mein.
how_it_works: HELLO handler version validate karta hai, optional SETNAME process karta hai, `ctx.client.proto` set karta hai aur ek dict return karta hai. Encoder `dict` ko proto 3 mein `%` map, proto 2 mein flat array banata hai.
in_this_project: `commands/server_cmds.py::hello`, `server.py::ClientState.proto` (default 2), `protocol.py::encode`. Tests: `test_encode_resp2_and_resp3` (wire bytes) aur `test_resp3_client` (redis-py `protocol=3` se HGETALL dict aur SMEMBERS set). Note: `conftest.py` ka default fixture deliberately `protocol=2` use karta hai.
code_example:
# real: tests/test_protocol.py
assert encode({b"f": b"v"}, 2) == b"*2
$1
f
$1
v
"
assert encode({b"f": b"v"}, 3) == b"%1
$1
f
$1
v
"
assert encode(RespSet([b"a"]), 3) == b"~1
$1
a
"
assert encode(None, 2) == b"$-1
" and encode(None, 3) == b"_
"
advantages: Commands protocol-agnostic; ek jagah encoding logic
disadvantages: Har naye type ke liye encoder dono branches maintain karna
RESP3 push messages/attributes implement nahi
common_mistakes: HELLO reply ko purane proto mein encode kar dena
Protocol ko global setting banana -- yeh per connection hai
dict ko RESP2 mein bhi map ki tarah bhejna
follow_up_questions: Agar client HELLO na bheje toh?
RESP3 push type kis feature ke liye hai?
HELLO ka reply kis protocol mein encode hota hai aur kyun?

question: Why are minidis command handlers synchronous functions, and how does that make every command atomic?
answer_hinglish:
Kyunki asyncio cooperative hai: ek task sirf `await` pe control chhodta hai. Agar handler ke andar koi `await` hi nahi hai, toh jab tak handler return nahi karta, event loop kisi doosre client ka code chala hi nahi sakta. Matlab har command apne aap atomic hai -- read-modify-write (jaise INCR: padho, +1, likho) ke beech koi doosra INCR interleave nahi ho sakta. Lock, mutex, CAS -- kuch nahi chahiye.

minidis mein yeh rule explicitly design kiya gaya hai. `commands/__init__.py` ka docstring kehta hai: "Every handler is a plain (synchronous) function ... Because handlers never await, the asyncio loop can't switch to another client in the middle of a command." `Server.execute` ka docstring: "Never awaits -> atomic with respect to other clients." `@command` decorator `def` functions register karta hai, `async def` nahi.

Proof: `test_concurrent_incr_is_exact` -- 50 alag clients, har ek 200 INCR, result exactly `10000`. Agar race hoti toh lost updates se kam aata.

Yeh guarantee kab toot ti? Agar koi future developer handler mein `await` daal de (jaise disk se kuch padhna), toh us point pe switch hoga aur atomicity gayi. Isliye slow I/O (fsync, snapshot write) handler ke bahar ya thread mein hota hai. Aur yeh sirf ek command ki atomicity hai -- multiple commands ke beech (MULTI/EXEC) nahi; woh implement nahi hai.
why_needed: Counters, rate limiters, inventory -- sab read-modify-write hain; bina atomicity ke lost updates hote hain.
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek hi cashier wala counter: ek customer ka bill poora hone tak doosra customer beech mein nahi aa sakta, toh hisaab kabhi mix nahi hota.
how_it_works: Event loop -> `_handle_client` task -> `execute(args)` (sync) -> handler (sync) -> return. Pura chain bina suspension point ke, toh doosre tasks tab tak ready queue mein wait karte hain.
in_this_project: `commands/__init__.py::command` decorator, `Server.execute`, `strings.py::_incr`. Downside ka proof bhi hai: `test_slow_command_blocks_all_clients` mein `DEBUG SLEEP 0.3` (jo `time.sleep` karta hai) chalne pe doosre client ka PING bhi ~0.3s rukta hai.
code_example:
# real: tests/test_concurrency.py
async def test_concurrent_incr_is_exact(server):
    clients = [client_for(server) for _ in range(50)]
    async def worker(c):
        for _ in range(200):
            await c.incr("counter")
    await asyncio.gather(*[worker(c) for c in clients])
    assert await clients[0].get("counter") == b"10000"
disadvantages: Ek slow command sab ko block karta hai
Ek CPU core tak limited
common_mistakes: Handler ko async bana dena 'modern' lagne ke liye
Atomicity ko multi-command transactions tak extend samajhna
time.sleep jaisi blocking calls handler mein daalna
follow_up_questions: Yeh guarantee multi-threaded server mein kaise milti?
MULTI/EXEC isi model mein kaise banaoge?
Slow command ka impact kaise measure karoge?

question: What is lazy expiration, and where does minidis apply it?
answer_hinglish:
Lazy (passive) expiration ka matlab: expired key ko tab delete karo jab koi usse access kare. Har lookup pe check hota hai `expires[key] <= now`; agar haan, toh key ko wahin hata do aur caller ko "key nahi hai" bolo. Fayda: koi background kaam nahi, sirf ek dict lookup ka cost, aur user ko kabhi expired value nahi dikhti.

minidis mein yeh `Keyspace._expire_if_needed` mein hai, jo `lookup()` aur `exists()` dono se call hota hai -- matlab GET, EXISTS, TYPE, TTL, INCR, LPUSH sab is raste se jaate hain. Master pe expired key mili toh `_remove(key)`, `stats.expired_keys += 1`, aur `on_implicit_delete([b"DEL", key])` callback -- jisse yeh deletion AOF mein `DEL` ki tarah likhi jaati hai aur replicas ko bhi jaati hai. Interesting baat: ek read command (GET) bhi is tarah AOF mein ek write (DEL) paida kar sakta hai.

Replica pe behaviour alag hai: `is_replica` true ho toh function sirf `True` return karta hai (logically gone) lekin key physically nahi hatata -- master ke DEL ka wait karta hai.

Kamzori: jo key koi kabhi padhta hi nahi, woh lazy expiry se kabhi nahi hategi -- memory leak jaisa. Isliye active expiry bhi chahiye.

Test: `test_lazy_expiry_on_access` fake `Clock` se time aage badhata hai aur verify karta hai ki lookup `None` deta hai, key `data` se gayi aur `expired_keys == 1`.
why_needed: Expired data user ko kabhi na dikhe, aur cleanup ka cost sirf touched keys pe lage.
real_world_analogy: Jaise fridge mein doodh: expiry date tab check karte ho jab use karne nikalo; jo packet kabhi nikalte hi nahi woh peeche sadta rehta hai.
how_it_works: Har access path pehle `_expire_if_needed(key)` call karta hai. Expired + master -> remove + stats + DEL propagate. Expired + replica -> hide only.
in_this_project: `keyspace.py::_expire_if_needed`, `lookup`, `exists`. `Keyspace` ka `clock` field injectable hai (default `time.time()*1000`), isliye tests mein `Clock` class se time control hota hai.
advantages: Expired data kabhi return nahi hota
disadvantages: Unread keys memory mein padi rehti hain
Read path pe bhi write side effects (DEL propagation)
common_mistakes: Sirf lazy expiry pe rely karna
Replica pe bhi lazy delete kar dena (divergence)
Time ko inject na karke tests mein real sleep use karna
follow_up_questions: Unread keys ka kya? Active expiry kaise kaam karti hai?
Replica expired key ko kyun nahi hatata?
Read command AOF mein DEL kyun likhta hai?

question: Explain the active expiry algorithm in minidis: sampling 20 keys and the 25% rule. Why is it probabilistic?
answer_hinglish:
Active expiry background mein un keys ko hatati hai jinhe koi padh nahi raha. Naive tarika -- har cycle saari volatile keys scan karo -- O(N) hai aur lakhon keys pe event loop ko freeze kar dega. Isliye Redis (aur minidis) probabilistic approach use karte hain.

Algorithm (`Keyspace.active_expire_cycle`, cron se 10 baar per second): volatile keys (jinpe TTL hai) mein se 20 random keys sample karo, jo expired hain unhe delete karo. Ab decision: agar sample ka 25% se zyada hissa expired nikla, toh iska matlab hai keyspace mein abhi bahut garbage hai -- dobara round chalao. Agar 25% ya kam, toh ruk jao; bacha hua garbage itna kam hai ki agle cycle tak wait kar sakte hain. Ek cycle maximum 16 rounds tak hi chalta hai (`max_rounds=16`), taaki ek cycle bhi loop ko zyada der block na kare.

Probabilistic kyun kaam karta hai: random sample population ka estimate hai. Agar 20 mein se 2 expired, toh roughly 10% keys expired hain -- memory "converge" karti hai ek bounded garbage ratio pe, bina sab scan kiye. Cost per cycle bounded hai (max 16 x 20 = 320 key checks).

Test: `test_active_expiry_removes_keys_nobody_reads` -- 1000 keys TTL ke saath aur 100 persistent, clock aage, cycles chalao jab tak `expires` khali na ho: sirf 100 persistent bachi, `expired_keys == 1000`. Replica pe yeh function seedha 0 return karta hai.
why_needed: Bina active expiry ke write-once-read-never keys (sessions, OTPs) memory bhar dete hain; full scan karna single-threaded server ko freeze karega.
real_world_analogy: Jaise ek bade godown mein inspector roz 20 random dabbe check karta hai; agar 5 se zyada kharab mile toh aur check karta hai, warna maan leta hai ki zyada kharab maal nahi bacha.
how_it_works: Sample `RandomSet.sample(20)` se (with replacement, toh `set(sample)` se dedupe), expired filter, `_expire_if_needed` har ek pe (jo DEL propagate karta hai), aur `len(expired) <= len(sample) // 4` pe break.
in_this_project: `keyspace.py::active_expire_cycle(sample_size=20, max_rounds=16)`, `server.py::_cron` usse har tick (`hz=10`, `ServerConfig.hz`) call karta hai. `INFO stats` mein `active_expire_cycles` counter dikhta hai.
advantages: Adaptive: jyada garbage pe zyada rounds
disadvantages: Kuch expired keys kuch der memory mein rehti hain
Random hai -- exact timing guarantee nahi
Mass expiry pe bhi max 16 rounds/tick tak hi kaam
common_mistakes: Saari keys scan karna
Persistent keys ko bhi sample karna (waste)
Round limit na lagana
follow_up_questions: 25% threshold badla toh kya trade-off?
Lakhon keys ek saath expire hon toh?
Random sampling O(1) kaise kiya?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: CPU vs memory trade-off: zyada rounds/samples = jaldi memory free lekin event loop pe zyada time. 25% threshold aur 16 rounds is balance ke knobs hain. Redis isme time budget bhi lagata hai (har cycle ka max CPU percent); minidis sirf round count se bound karta hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar ek saath million keys expire hon (jaise sab ek hi TTL ke saath bani), toh har tick sirf ~320 keys check hongi -- garbage dheere saaf hoga aur used_memory thodi der high rahega, jo eviction trigger kar sakta hai. Clock jump (NTP) se bahut keys ek saath expired dikh sakti hain.
advanced.alternatives: Timer wheel / min-heap by expiry time: exact expiry, lekin har TTL set pe O(log n) aur extra memory. Redis 7 ne bhi sampling hi rakha, plus incremental bucket scanning.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x keys pe bhi per-cycle cost same rehta hai (bounded), lekin convergence ka time badhta hai. 100x pe `hz` badhana ya time-budget based loop (Redis ka fast/slow cycle) chahiye. Python mein per-key check mehnga hai, toh C wale Redis se kam keys/sec saaf hongi.
advanced.production_improvements: Time budget (jaise 25ms per 100ms) based cycle, `expired_stale_perc` jaisa metric INFO mein, TTL jitter recommend karna taaki mass expiry na ho, aur adaptive hz.

question: What eviction policies does minidis support, and when would you choose each?
answer_hinglish:
Eviction tab hota hai jab `maxmemory` set hai aur write command aata hai jabki estimated memory limit se upar hai. minidis chaar policies deta hai (`EvictionPolicy` enum):

1. `noeviction` (default): kuch delete nahi karta, write pe `OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'.` error deta hai. Reads chalte rehte hain. Jab data primary hai aur kho nahi sakte -- jaise queues, counters jinka koi source nahi.
2. `allkeys-lru`: saari keys mein se least recently used hatao -- exact LRU, OrderedDict ki pehli key. Pure cache ke liye best, jahan har cheez rebuild ho sakti hai.
3. `volatile-lru`: sirf TTL wali keys mein se, 5 random sample karke sabse purani access wali hatao (Redis-style approximate LRU). Jab ek hi instance mein cache keys (TTL ke saath) aur persistent data dono hain -- persistent safe rehta hai.
4. `volatile-ttl`: TTL wali keys mein se jo sabse jaldi expire hone wali hai use hatao (sample se). Logic: woh waise bhi jaane wali thi.

Important gotcha: volatile policies ko agar koi TTL wali key nahi mili toh woh kuch evict nahi kar sakti aur OOM hi deti hain -- `test_volatile_policy_cannot_free_persistent_keys` yeh prove karta hai.

Eviction check `Server.execute` mein har write se pehle hota hai (Redis bhi aise hi karta hai), aur har evicted key `DEL` ke roop mein AOF aur replicas tak propagate hoti hai.
why_needed: Galat policy = ya toh important data silently gayab (allkeys-lru on primary store) ya cache full hoke writes fail (noeviction on cache).
real_world_analogy: Jaise almaari bhar gayi: noeviction = naya saman lene se mana; allkeys-lru = sabse kam use hone wali cheez nikaal do; volatile-ttl = jo cheez waise bhi kal phenkni thi woh aaj phenk do.
how_it_works: `execute` -> `evict_until_fits(maxmemory, policy, samples)` -> loop jab tak `used_memory > maxmemory`: `_pick_victim` -> `_remove` -> `evicted_keys += 1` -> DEL propagate. Victim None mila toh False -> OOM error.
in_this_project: `keyspace.py::EvictionPolicy`, `evict_until_fits`, `_pick_victim`; `config.py` mein `maxmemory_samples=5`. Runtime pe `CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru` se badal sakte ho. Tests: `test_allkeys_lru_evicts_least_recently_used`, `test_volatile_ttl_evicts_soonest_expiring_and_spares_persistent`, `test_noeviction_returns_oom_error`, `test_allkeys_lru_server_keeps_hot_key`.
advantages: Reads OOM mein bhi chalte hain
disadvantages: allkeys-lfu, allkeys-random, volatile-random implement nahi
Memory estimate hai, real RSS nahi
common_mistakes: Cache pe noeviction chhod dena (writes fail)
Primary store pe allkeys-lru (silent data loss)
volatile policy lagana jab keys pe TTL hi nahi
follow_up_questions: Exact LRU vs sampled LRU ka trade-off?
LFU kab LRU se better hai?
Replica pe eviction kyun nahi hota?

question: Compare snapshots and the AOF in minidis. What does each protect against, and what does each cost?
answer_hinglish:
Dono persistence mechanisms hain lekin alag sawal ka jawab dete hain.

Snapshot (`dump.mdb`) poore dataset ki point-in-time binary photo hai. Fayde: compact file, restart pe fast load (sirf deserialize, koi command re-execute nahi), aur backups ke liye perfect -- ek file copy karo. Nuksan: last snapshot ke baad ke saare writes crash pe lose. Trigger: `SAVE` (blocking), `BGSAVE`, ya save rules jaise `300 100` (300s mein 100 changes).

AOF (`appendonly.aof`) har write command ka log hai, RESP format mein, execution order mein. Fayda: durability fine-grained -- `always` mein koi acknowledged write lose nahi, `everysec` mein ~1s, `no` mein OS ki marzi. Nuksan: file hamesha badhti hai (500 INCR = 500 entries, isliye `BGREWRITEAOF`), replay slow hai kyunki har command dobara chalana padta hai, aur `always` mein fsync latency har batch pe.

minidis mein restart pe AOF ko prefer kiya jaata hai agar enabled hai aur exist karti hai, kyunki woh usually zyada up-to-date hoti hai (`_load_from_disk`). `DEPLOYMENT.md` dono rakhne ki salah deta hai: AOF everysec durability ke liye, snapshots fast restart aur easy backups ke liye. Real Redis 7 dono ko combine karta hai (RDB preamble + AOF tail); minidis clarity ke liye inhe alag rakhta hai.
why_needed: Interview mein "Redis data kaise persist karta hai" classic hai; trade-off clearly bol paana zaroori hai.
real_world_analogy: Snapshot = har shaam bank balance ki photo; AOF = har transaction ki passbook entry. Photo se jaldi pata chalta hai balance, passbook se kuch miss nahi hota.
how_it_works: Snapshot: `snapshot.dump(ks)` -> bytes -> `write_atomic`. AOF: har write ke baad `_propagate` -> `aof.append(encode_command(cmd))` -> batch end pe flush/fsync policy ke hisaab se.
in_this_project: `persistence/snapshot.py` (format + CRC + atomic write), `persistence/aof.py` (append, fsync, replay, rewrite), `server.py::_check_save_rules` aur `_load_from_disk`. Tests: `test_snapshot_restart`, `test_aof_restart_without_snapshot` (always/everysec/no parametrized).
advantages: Dono saath use ho sakte hain
disadvantages: Snapshot: data loss window minutes ka
AOF: badi file, slow replay, rewrite chahiye
always fsync throughput kam karta hai
common_mistakes: Snapshot ko hi durable maan lena
AOF rewrite configure na karna aur disk bhar jaana
Restart priority (AOF vs snapshot) na jaanna
follow_up_questions: AOF aur snapshot dono hain toh restart pe kaunsa load?
AOF rewrite kaise kaam karta hai?
everysec mein data loss kab hota hai?

question: Give an overview of master-replica replication in minidis: what messages flow, and what consistency does it provide?
answer_hinglish:
minidis mein simplified Redis-style asynchronous replication hai, chaar steps mein:

1. Replica master se TCP connect karke `SYNC` bhejta hai (`ReplicaLink._sync_once`).
2. Master `_serve_replica` mein synchronously `snapshot.dump(self.ks)` banata hai aur `$<len>\r\n<snapshot bytes>` bhejta hai. Replica `readexactly` se payload padh ke `snapshot.load` karta hai -- poora dataset replace.
3. Uske baad master har propagated write command (wahi bytes jo AOF mein jaate hain) replica ko stream karta hai; replica unhe `apply_from_master` se `execute(..., from_master=True)` chalata hai, jo READONLY check bypass karta hai.
4. Replica har second `REPLCONF ACK <offset>` bhejta hai; master `INFO replication` mein `lag_bytes = master_repl_offset - ack_offset` dikhata hai.

Consistency: asynchronous, eventually consistent. Master client ko reply replicas ke confirm karne ka wait kiye bina deta hai, toh replica thoda peeche ho sakta hai (stale reads), aur master crash ho jaye toh jo writes acknowledge hue lekin stream nahi hue woh lose ho sakte hain. `WAIT` implement nahi hai.

Extra rules: replica read-only hai (`READONLY` error), replica khud keys expire nahi karta (master ke DEL ka wait), slow replica ka buffer 64MB cross kare toh disconnect, connection toote toh exponential backoff (0.1s -> 2s) se reconnect aur hamesha full sync -- PSYNC nahi hai. `REPLICAOF NO ONE` se manual promotion.
why_needed: Read scaling aur failover ke liye copy chahiye; aur interview mein async replication ka data-loss window explain karna expected hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise head office ka register aur branch ki photocopy: pehle poori copy di, phir har nayi entry phone pe bata di. Phone pe batane se pehle head office jal gaya toh woh entry branch pe nahi pahunchi.
how_it_works: Full sync (snapshot) + command stream + periodic ACKs. Stream mein wahi RESP-encoded commands jaate hain jo `_propagate` AOF ke liye banata hai, isliye relative TTL absolute aur expiries DEL ban ke jaati hain.
in_this_project: `replication.py::ReplicaLink` (`_run`, `_sync_once`, `_ack_loop`), `server.py::_serve_replica`, `_propagate`, `_flush_replication`, `become_replica_of`, `promote_to_master`, `_check_replica_buffers`. Tests: `tests/test_replication.py` ke 6 tests.
code_example:
replica -> master : SYNC
master  -> replica: $<len>\r\n<snapshot bytes>        (full copy)
master  -> replica: *N\r\n...  write commands, forever  (stream)
replica -> master : REPLCONF ACK <offset>  every second
advantages: Simple protocol, hamesha correct full sync
disadvantages: Failover pe acknowledged writes lose ho sakte hain
Har reconnect full sync (no PSYNC)
Automatic failover nahi
common_mistakes: Async replication ko durable maan lena
Replica se read karke read-your-writes expect karna
Replica pe writes allow kar dena
follow_up_questions: Data loss window exactly kab hota hai?
PSYNC kaise implement karoge?
Replica khud expire kyun nahi karta?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Async vs sync: async mein write latency sirf master ki, lekin durability across nodes nahi. Sync (har write pe replica ACK ka wait) mein latency RTT jitni badhegi aur replica down ho toh writes ruk sakte hain. minidis Redis ki default (async) choose karta hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Master crash -> unstreamed writes lost. Network partition -> replica backoff se retry karta rehta hai, stale data serve karta hai. Slow replica -> 64MB buffer pe disconnect aur full sync loop (agar network hi slow hai toh baar baar full sync).
advanced.alternatives: Raft/Paxos jaise consensus (majority ACK) -- strong consistency lekin zyada latency aur complexity. Redis ka WAIT command semi-sync deta hai. Postgres jaisa synchronous_commit mode.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x dataset pe har full sync (snapshot in-loop + network) mehenga ho jaata hai -- PSYNC zaroori. Zyada replicas pe master ka outgoing bandwidth N guna; chained replication ya fan-out tree chahiye.
advanced.production_improvements: PSYNC with backlog + replid, WAIT N timeout, Sentinel-style automatic failover, replica priority, min-replicas-to-write (agar replicas nahi toh writes reject).

question: Walk through Server._handle_client. How does it process one read from the socket, and why is it structured that way?
answer_hinglish:
`_handle_client` ek connection ka poora lifecycle hai. Start mein `ClientState` banta hai (id, addr, proto=2) aur `self.clients` mein register hota hai, ek naya `Parser` milta hai. Phir loop:

1. `data = await reader.read(65536)` -- khali bytes matlab client ne connection band kiya, loop break.
2. `parser.feed(data)`, phir inner loop `while (args := parser.get_command()) is not None`.
3. Special cases: `SYNC`/`PSYNC` aaya toh ab tak ke replies flush karke connection `_serve_replica` ko de diya jaata hai (yeh connection ab replica hai). `QUIT` pe `OK` aur `close_after`. Baaki sab `self.execute(args, client)` aur reply `encode(..., client.proto)` karke `replies` list mein.
4. `ProtocolError` aaya toh error reply aur `close_after = True` -- malformed stream resync nahi ho sakti.
5. Batch ke baad durability: AOF hai toh `always` policy pe `self.aof.fsync()` (reply se pehle disk), warna `flush()`.
6. `writer.write(b"".join(replies))` aur `await writer.drain()`.

Structure ka reason: ek read mein jitne commands aaye unka ek batch -- ek fsync (group commit) aur ek socket write. `drain()` backpressure deta hai: agar client replies nahi padh raha, toh task yahan rukta hai aur us client ke naye commands padhna band -- server memory nahi phulti. `finally` mein client `clients` aur `replicas` dono se hata diya jaata hai aur writer close.
why_needed: Yeh function server ka hot path hai; durability ordering (fsync before reply) aur backpressure dono yahin decide hote hain.
real_world_analogy: Jaise post office counter: ek customer ke saare letters ek saath lo, sab pe stamp lagao, ek baar register mein entry karo, aur saari receipts ek saath do.
how_it_works: Per-read batch processing: parse all -> execute all -> persist (fsync/flush) -> reply all -> drain. Execute sync hai, toh poora batch atomically ek-ek command chalta hai; sirf `read` aur `drain` pe task suspend hota hai.
in_this_project: `server.py::_handle_client`. Note karo `writer.write(b"".join(replies))` SYNC branch mein bhi hota hai -- taaki SYNC se pehle ke pipelined commands ke replies kho na jaayein. Exceptions `ConnectionError` aur `IncompleteReadError` silently handle.
advantages: Group commit aur single write per batch
disadvantages: `always` mode mein fsync event loop mein synchronous -- sab clients us dauraan rukte hain
Per-client query buffer limit nahi
common_mistakes: Reply pehle bhejna aur fsync baad mein (durability guarantee tootegi)
drain() bhool jana -- slow reader pe unbounded memory
Protocol error ke baad connection open rakhna
follow_up_questions: fsync event loop ko block karta hai -- kya improve karoge?
Batch size bahut bada ho toh latency pe asar?
SYNC ke baad yeh connection kaise behave karta hai?

question: What does Server.execute do, step by step, for a single command?
answer_hinglish:
`execute(args, client, from_master=False)` ek command ka central dispatcher hai, aur deliberately sync hai.

1. Counters: `total_commands` aur `client.commands` badhao (INFO aur CLIENT LIST ke liye).
2. Lookup: `REGISTRY.get(args[0].upper())` -- nahi mila toh `ERR unknown command '...'`.
3. `check_arity(cmd, args)` -- positive arity exact count, negative arity "kam se kam".
4. Replica guard: command write hai, server replica hai (`replica_link is not None`) aur command master se nahi aaya, toh `READONLY You can't write against a read only replica.`
5. Memory guard: write command aur `maxmemory` set (aur from_master nahi), toh `evict_until_fits` -- fail hua toh `OOM command not allowed...`. Note: eviction check write ke pehle hota hai, Redis jaisa.
6. `Context(self, self.ks, client)` banao aur `cmd.handler(ctx, args)` chalao. `RespError` ko catch karke as reply return (connection open rehta hai).
7. Write command hai toh propagation: `ctx.propagate` None hai toh original args, warna handler ne jo rewrite kiya (jaise SET + PEXPIREAT, ya `[]` matlab kuch nahi badla). Har command `_propagate` (AOF + replicas). Agar kuch bhi propagate hua toh `persistence.dirty += 1`.

Ek design point: errors exceptions se flow hote hain (`raise RespError`), lekin `execute` unhe return value bana deta hai -- `encode` RespError ko `-ERR ...` mein badal deta hai. Isse handlers mein error handling simple rehti hai.
why_needed: Har command ke cross-cutting rules (arity, read-only, OOM, propagation, dirty tracking) ek jagah hain -- handlers sirf business logic likhte hain.
real_world_analogy: Jaise airport security: ticket check, ID check, baggage weight check -- sab gate pe, airline staff ko baar baar nahi karna padta.
how_it_works: Registry dict -> Command dataclass (handler, arity, write flag) -> guards -> handler -> propagation. `from_master=True` sirf replica apply path pe aata hai, jo READONLY aur eviction dono skip karta hai.
in_this_project: `server.py::execute`, `commands/__init__.py::check_arity`, `Command` dataclass ka `write` flag. `apply_from_master` replica side se `execute(args, None, from_master=True)` call karta hai aur error ho toh `replica_apply_failed` log karta hai.
disadvantages: Eviction check estimate pe based; ek bada write maxmemory cross kar sakta hai (check pehle hota hai, baad mein nahi)
Command metadata (flags) minimal hai -- Redis ke paas bahut zyada flags hain
common_mistakes: Eviction write ke baad check karna
Replica apply path pe READONLY lagana (stream toot jayega)
Dirty counter har command pe badhana chahe kuch na badla ho
follow_up_questions: from_master flag kyun chahiye?
Write command ne kuch nahi badla toh propagate kyun nahi?
Unknown command ka error format kya hai aur kyun?

question: How does the command registry work, and what does the arity convention mean?
answer_hinglish:
Har command ek decorator se register hota hai: `@command("SET", -3, write=True)`. Decorator function ko `REGISTRY` dict mein `Command(name, handler, arity, write)` ki tarah daal deta hai, key uppercase naam. `commands/__init__.py` ke end mein `from . import hashes, keys, lists, server_cmds, sets, strings` hai -- yeh import sirf side effect ke liye hai, taaki saare decorators chal jaayein aur registry bhar jaye.

Arity Redis wala convention follow karta hai, aur command naam bhi count hota hai:
- Positive arity = exact args. `GET` arity 2: `GET key`. `INCRBY` 3: `INCRBY key n`.
- Negative arity = minimum `abs(arity)`. `SET` -3: kam se kam `SET key value`, aage options. `DEL` -2: `DEL k1 [k2 ...]`. `PING` -1: `PING` ya `PING msg`.

`check_arity` mismatch pe `ERR wrong number of arguments for 'get' command` deta hai -- exactly Redis wala message, toh clients ka error parsing kaam karta hai.

`write` flag teen cheezein control karta hai: replica pe READONLY rejection, AOF/replica propagation, aur eviction check. Ek real bug yahin se aaya tha: `BGSAVE` ka arity pehle exact 1 tha, lekin redis-py `BGSAVE SCHEDULE` bhejta hai -- arity -1 karke fix kiya, aur handler extra arg ko accept karke turant start karta hai.
why_needed: Ek jagah metadata se dispatch fast aur consistent rehta hai; naya command add karna ek function + decorator hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise restaurant ka menu card: har dish ka naam, kitne side items allowed, aur "veg/non-veg" flag -- kitchen sirf card dekh ke decide karta hai.
how_it_works: Import time pe decorators chalte hain -> dict bharta hai. Runtime pe O(1) dict lookup. Arity check do conditions: `arity > 0 and n != arity` ya `arity < 0 and n < -arity`.
in_this_project: `commands/__init__.py::command`, `REGISTRY`, `check_arity`. `COMMAND COUNT` `len(REGISTRY)` return karta hai. AOF replay (`server.py::_apply_replay`) bhi isi registry se handler uthata hai.
disadvantages: Import side effects se registration -- import bhool gaye toh command gayab
Arity sirf count check karta hai, option syntax handler ko khud check karna padta hai
common_mistakes: Arity mein command naam ginna bhool jana
Write flag galat lagana (propagation/READONLY toot jayega)
follow_up_questions: write flag galat laga diya toh kya bugs aayenge?
BGSAVE SCHEDULE wala bug kaise pakda?
Command flags aur kya ho sakte hain (Redis mein)?

question: How does Context.rewrite control what gets written to the AOF and sent to replicas? Give concrete examples.
answer_hinglish:
Har handler ko ek `Context` milta hai jisme `propagate: list[list[bytes]] | None = None` field hai. Rule: `None` matlab "original command jaisa hai waisa propagate karo"; list matlab "inke bajaye yeh commands bhejo"; khali list matlab "kuch nahi badla, kuch mat bhejo". Handler `ctx.rewrite(*cmds)` call karke yeh set karta hai, aur `Server.execute` write commands ke baad isi ko `_propagate` karta hai.

Examples code se:
- `SET k v EX 60` -> `ctx.rewrite([b"SET", key, value], [b"PEXPIREAT", key, str(expire_at).encode()])`. Relative TTL absolute ban jaata hai, taaki AOF replay ya late replica apply karne pe fresh 60s na mil jaye.
- `SET k v NX` jab key already hai -> `ctx.rewrite()` (khali) -> kuch propagate nahi, aur `dirty` bhi nahi badhta (`if cmds:`).
- `EXPIRE k 60` -> `PEXPIREAT k <abs>`; past time ka expire -> key delete aur `DEL k` propagate.
- `GETDEL k` -> key thi toh `DEL k`, warna kuch nahi.
- `LPOP` pe key nahi -> `ctx.rewrite()`.
- `FLUSHALL` -> `FLUSHDB` (minidis single DB hai).

Yeh pattern Redis ke `rewriteClientCommandVector`/`alsoPropagate` jaisa hai. Benefit: replay deterministic hota hai -- AOF ya replica pe command chalane ka result time ya existing state pe depend nahi karta jitna possible ho.
why_needed: Non-deterministic commands (relative time, conditional writes) ko as-is log karna replay pe alag result de sakta hai -- data divergence.
real_world_analogy: Jaise accountant "kal se 30 din" nahi likhta, likhta hai "15 December tak" -- register kabhi bhi padho, matlab same rehta hai.
how_it_works: Handler state change karta hai aur effect ka deterministic description `ctx.propagate` mein daalta hai. `execute`: `cmds = [args] if ctx.propagate is None else ctx.propagate`, har ek `_propagate`, `if cmds: dirty += 1`.
in_this_project: `commands/__init__.py::Context.rewrite`, `strings.py::set_` (PEXPIREAT comment ke saath), `keys.py::_expire_generic`, `strings.py::getdel`, `keys.py::flushdb`. Test `test_aof_stores_absolute_expiry` verify karta hai ki AOF mein `PEXPIREAT` hai aur `EX` kahin nahi.
code_example:
# real, trimmed: minidis/commands/strings.py::set_
if (nx and exists) or (xx and not exists):
    ctx.rewrite()  # nothing changed -> nothing to propagate
    return old if want_get else None
ctx.ks.store(key, value, keep_ttl=keepttl)
if expire_at is not None:
    ctx.ks.set_expire_at(key, expire_at)
    ctx.rewrite([b"SET", key, value], [b"PEXPIREAT", key, str(expire_at).encode()])
advantages: No-op writes AOF/replicas pe load nahi daalte
disadvantages: Har expiring SET ke liye ek extra AOF entry
Har handler ko yaad rakhna padta hai ki rewrite karna hai -- bhool gaye toh original args jaate hain
common_mistakes: Relative TTL ko as-is AOF mein likhna
Failed conditional write ko bhi propagate karna
rewrite() aur rewrite([]) ka matlab confuse karna
follow_up_questions: INCR ko kaise propagate karte ho -- as INCR ya SET?
SPOP/random commands ko deterministic kaise banaoge?
PERSIST missing key pe kya propagate hota hai?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Effect-based propagation (final value bhejna, jaise INCR -> SET) zyada deterministic hai lekin bade collections pe bandwidth zyada. Command-based (as-is) sasta hai lekin non-deterministic commands ke liye rewrite chahiye. minidis hybrid hai: default as-is, rewrite jahan zaroori.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar koi handler rewrite bhool jaye aur command non-deterministic ho (jaise future mein SPOP add kiya), toh master aur replica ka data silently diverge karega -- koi error nahi aayega. Abhi `PERSIST` missing key pe bhi original args propagate karta hai, jo harmless no-op hai lekin dirty badha deta hai.
advanced.alternatives: Redis 7 Lua/functions ke liye effects replication use karta hai (script ke andar ke writes bhejta hai, script nahi). Postgres logical replication row changes bhejta hai, SQL nahi.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Volume badhe toh extra PEXPIREAT entries AOF size badhate hain; rewrite frequency badhani padegi. Replication bandwidth bhi utni badhegi.
advanced.production_improvements: Ek test harness jo har write command ko master pe chala ke uska propagated stream ek fresh keyspace pe replay kare aur state compare kare (property-based testing) -- isse rewrite bhoolne wale bugs automatically pakde jaayenge.
